claim: Bathymodiolus mussels live in symbiosis with intracellular sulfur-oxidizing (SOX) bacteria that provide them with nutrition.
source: Bathymodiolus mussels live in symbiosis with intracellular sulfur-oxidizing (SOX) bacteria that provide them with nutrition.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Up to 35% of the Bathymodiolus SOX symbiont genes may have been acquired by horizontal gene transfer.
source: Comparison of these symbiont genomes with those of their closest relatives revealed that the symbionts have undergone genome rearrangements, and up to 35% of their genes may have been acquired by horizontal gene transfer.
evidence: This is based on codon usage analysis presented in Table 1 and discussed in the results.

claim: Many of the genes specific to the Bathymodiolus SOX symbionts are homologs of virulence genes.
source: Many of the genes specific to the symbionts were homologs of virulence genes.
evidence: This is based on comparative genomic analysis and annotation described in the results section.

claim: The Bathymodiolus SOX symbionts contain an abundant and diverse array of genes similar to insecticidal toxins of nematode and aphid symbionts, and toxins of pathogens such as Yersinia and Vibrio.
source: We discovered an abundant and diverse array of genes similar to insecticidal toxins of nematode and aphid symbionts, and toxins of pathogens such as Yersinia and Vibrio.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis (Figure 3) and sequence similarity networks (Figure 4).

claim: The SOX symbionts express toxin-related genes (TRGs) in their hosts.
source: Transcriptomics and proteomics revealed that the SOX symbionts express the toxin-related genes (TRGs) in their hosts.
evidence: This is demonstrated by transcriptome and proteome data presented in the results section and Table 4.

claim: The symbionts may use TRGs in beneficial interactions with their host, including protection against parasites.
source: We hypothesize that the symbionts use these TRGs in beneficial interactions with their host, including protection against parasites.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on the data and discussed extensively in the discussion section.

claim: Bathymodiolus mussels dominate deep-sea hydrothermal vents and cold seeps worldwide.
source: Mussels of the genus Bathymodiolus dominate deep-sea hydrothermal vents and cold seeps worldwide.
evidence: This is supported by citations to von Cosel, 2002 and Van Dover et al., 2002.

claim: The key to Bathymodiolus mussels' ecological and evolutionary success is their symbiosis with chemosynthetic bacteria.
source: The key to their ecological and evolutionary success is their symbiosis with chemosynthetic bacteria that provide them with nutrition (von Cosel, 2002; Van Dover et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to von Cosel, 2002 and Van Dover et al., 2002.

claim: Bathymodiolus mussels host their symbionts inside specialized gill epithelial cells called bacteriocytes.
source: Bathymodiolus mussels host their symbionts inside specialized gill epithelial cells called bacteriocytes (Cavanaugh et al., 2006; Petersen and Dubilier, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cavanaugh et al., 2006 and Petersen and Dubilier, 2009.

claim: Some Bathymodiolus mussel species associate exclusively with sulfur-oxidizing (SOX) symbionts.
source: Some mussel species associate exclusively with sulfur-oxidizing (SOX) symbionts that use reduced sulfur compounds and sometimes hydrogen as an energy source, and carbon dioxide as a carbon source.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fisher et al., 1993; Distel et al., 1995; Duperron et al., 2006; Dubilier et al., 2008; Petersen et al., 2011.

claim: Some Bathymodiolus mussel species have only methane-oxidizing (MOX) symbionts.
source: Some have only methane-oxidizing (MOX) symbionts that use methane as an energy source and carbon source.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fisher et al., 1993; Distel et al., 1995; Duperron et al., 2006; Dubilier et al., 2008; Petersen et al., 2011.

claim: Some Bathymodiolus mussel species host both SOX and MOX symbionts in a dual symbiosis.
source: Some mussel species host both types in a dual symbiosis (Fisher et al., 1993; Distel et al., 1995; Duperron et al., 2006; Dubilier et al., 2008; Petersen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fisher et al., 1993; Distel et al., 1995; Duperron et al., 2006; Dubilier et al., 2008; Petersen et al., 2011.

claim: In all Bathymodiolus species except one, a single 16S rRNA phylotype for each type of symbiont (SOX or MOX) is found in the gills.
source: In all species except one, a single 16S rRNA phylotype for each type of symbiont (SOX or MOX) is found in the gills (Dubilier et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dubilier et al., 2008.

claim: There are more than 30 described Bathymodiolus species.
source: There are more than 30 described Bathymodiolus species, and most associate with a characteristic symbiont phylotype, which is not found in other species (Duperron et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Duperron et al., 2013.

claim: Most Bathymodiolus species associate with a characteristic symbiont phylotype, which is not found in other species.
source: There are more than 30 described Bathymodiolus species, and most associate with a characteristic symbiont phylotype, which is not found in other species (Duperron et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Duperron et al., 2013.

claim: The molecular mechanisms that underpin the specificity of Bathymodiolus-symbiont associations are still unknown.
source: Although these associations are clearly very specific, the molecular mechanisms that underpin this specificity are still unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: No chemosynthetic symbiont has ever been obtained in pure culture.
source: No chemosynthetic symbiont has ever been obtained in pure culture.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of the field.

claim: The Bathymodiolus symbionts are assumed to be horizontally transmitted.
source: The Bathymodiolus symbionts are assumed to be horizontally transmitted, which means that each new host generation must take up their symbionts from the surrounding environment or co-occurring adults (Won et al., 2003b; Kadar et al., 2005; DeChaine et al., 2006; Fontanez and Cavanaugh, 2014; Wentrup et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Won et al., 2003b; Kadar et al., 2005; DeChaine et al., 2006; Fontanez and Cavanaugh, 2014; Wentrup et al., 2014.

claim: The Bathymodiolus symbionts seem to induce a loss of microvilli on the cells they colonize.
source: Indeed, like many intracellular pathogens, the Bathymodiolus symbionts seem to induce a loss of microvilli on the cells they colonize (Cossart and Sansonetti, 2004; Bhavsar et al., 2007; Haglund and Welch, 2011; Wentrup et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cossart and Sansonetti, 2004; Bhavsar et al., 2007; Haglund and Welch, 2011; Wentrup et al., 2014.

claim: The Bathymodiolus symbionts achieve dense populations inside the host cells.
source: Finally, the symbionts achieve dense populations inside the host cells (e.g., Duperron et al., 2006; Halary et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Duperron et al., 2006 and Halary et al., 2008.

claim: The Bathymodiolus SOX symbionts are not closely related to any known pathogens.
source: In contrast to the Sodalis symbionts of insects and the Vibrio symbionts of squid, the Bathymodiolus SOX symbionts are not closely related to any known pathogens.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The Bathymodiolus SOX symbionts are hypothesized to have evolved multiple times from free-living ancestors.
source: Moreover, because they fall interspersed between free-living SOX bacteria in 16S rRNA phylogenies, they are hypothesized to have evolved multiple times from free-living ancestors (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) (Petersen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and cited from Petersen et al., 2012.

claim: The closest free-living relatives of Bathymodiolus SOX symbionts are marine SOX bacteria called SUP05.
source: Their closest free-living relatives are marine SOX bacteria called SUP05, which are abundant in the world's oceans, particularly in oxygen minimum zones (OMZs) and hydrothermal plumes (Sunamura et al., 2004; Lavik et al., 2009; Walsh et al., 2009; Anantharaman et al., 2012; Wright et al., 2012; Petersen and Dubilier, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sunamura et al., 2004; Lavik et al., 2009; Walsh et al., 2009; Anantharaman et al., 2012; Wright et al., 2012; Petersen and Dubilier, 2014.

claim: SUP05 bacteria are abundant in the world's oceans, particularly in oxygen minimum zones (OMZs) and hydrothermal plumes.
source: Their closest free-living relatives are marine SOX bacteria called SUP05, which are abundant in the world's oceans, particularly in oxygen minimum zones (OMZs) and hydrothermal plumes (Sunamura et al., 2004; Lavik et al., 2009; Walsh et al., 2009; Anantharaman et al., 2012; Wright et al., 2012; Petersen and Dubilier, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sunamura et al., 2004; Lavik et al., 2009; Walsh et al., 2009; Anantharaman et al., 2012; Wright et al., 2012; Petersen and Dubilier, 2014.

claim: The Bathymodiolus SOX symbionts and SUP05 bacteria form a monophyletic clade together with the SOX symbionts of vesicomyid clams based on 16S rRNA gene phylogenies.
source: The Bathymodiolus SOX symbionts and SUP05 bacteria form a monophyletic clade together with the SOX symbionts of vesicomyid clams based on 16S rRNA gene phylogenies (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) (Distel et al., 1995; Petersen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and supported by citations to Distel et al., 1995 and Petersen et al., 2012.

claim: All members of the monophyletic group (mussel and clam symbionts, and SUP05) are capable of autotrophic growth.
source: All members of this monophyletic group (the mussel and clam symbionts, and SUP05) share similar core metabolic features. They are all capable of autotrophic growth, and all use reduced sulfur compounds as an energy source (Newton et al., 2008; Walsh et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Newton et al., 2008 and Walsh et al., 2009.

claim: All members of the monophyletic group (mussel and clam symbionts, and SUP05) use reduced sulfur compounds as an energy source.
source: All members of this monophyletic group (the mussel and clam symbionts, and SUP05) share similar core metabolic features. They are all capable of autotrophic growth, and all use reduced sulfur compounds as an energy source (Newton et al., 2008; Walsh et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Newton et al., 2008 and Walsh et al., 2009.

claim: SUP05 bacteria are exclusively free-living.
source: However, the major difference between these organisms is their lifestyle: SUP05 bacteria are exclusively free-living.
evidence: This is stated as a known fact about SUP05.

claim: The clam symbionts are exclusively host-associated and are vertically transmitted.
source: The clam symbionts are exclusively host-associated, are vertically transmitted, and have reduced genomes.
evidence: This is stated as a known fact about clam symbionts.

claim: The clam symbionts have reduced genomes.
source: The clam symbionts are exclusively host-associated, are vertically transmitted, and have reduced genomes.
evidence: This is supported by the genome size data in Table 1.

claim: The Bathymodiolus symbionts appear to have adapted to both host-associated and free-living niches.
source: The Bathymodiolus symbionts appear to have adapted to both niches, as they have a host-associated stage and are assumed to also have a free-living stage.
evidence: This is based on the horizontal transmission hypothesis and comparative analysis.

claim: The draft genomes of the Bathymodiolus SOX symbionts were 90.7–97.7% complete.
source: Despite different sequencing and assembly strategies, the draft genomes were 90.7–97.7% complete (Table 1).
evidence: This is based on CheckM analysis presented in Table 1.

claim: The total assembly sizes of the Bathymodiolus SOX symbiont genomes were between 1.7 and 2.3 Mbp.
source: The total assembly sizes were between 1.7 and 2.3 Mbp, on 52 to 506 contigs (Table 1).
evidence: This is shown in Table 1.

claim: The 16S rRNA genes from the two B. azoricus symbionts were 100% identical.
source: The 16S rRNA genes from the two B. azoricus symbionts were 100% identical and were 99.3% identical to BspSym.
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison of the 16S rRNA genes.

claim: The 16S rRNA genes from the two B. azoricus symbionts were 99.3% identical to BspSym.
source: The 16S rRNA genes from the two B. azoricus symbionts were 100% identical and were 99.3% identical to BspSym.
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison of the 16S rRNA genes.

claim: Bathymodiolus symbiont genomes were more similar to the free-living SUP05 than to the clam symbionts in terms of size and GC content.
source: Bathymodiolus symbiont genomes were more similar to the free-living SUP05 than to the clam symbionts in terms of size and GC content (Table 1).
evidence: This is based on comparison of genome statistics in Table 1.

claim: All three Bathymodiolus SOX symbiont genomes had a greater proportion of genes that may have been acquired through recent horizontal gene transfer compared to the clam symbionts.
source: Analysis of codon usage showed that all three Bathymodiolus SOX symbiont genomes had a greater proportion of genes that may have been acquired through recent horizontal gene transfer (HGT) compared to the clam symbionts Candidatus Vesicomyosocius okutanii, and Candidatus Ruthia magnifica (Table 1).
evidence: This is based on codon usage analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: BspSym lacked synteny compared to SUP05 and the clam symbionts.
source: BspSym, the genome that assembled into the fewest contigs, lacked synteny compared to SUP05 and the clam symbionts, as shown by whole genome alignment (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown by whole genome alignment in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The possibility of incorrect genome assembly for BspSym was ruled out for four regions by PCR amplification.
source: The possibility of incorrect genome assembly for BspSym was ruled out for four regions by PCR amplification of sequences spanning the regions without synteny.
evidence: This is based on PCR validation experiments described in the methods.

claim: The regions without genome synteny most likely represent true genome reshuffling in Bathymodiolus symbionts.
source: These regions without genome synteny therefore most likely represent true genome reshuffling in Bathymodiolus symbionts.
evidence: This is inferred from the PCR validation and genome comparison.

claim: The Bathymodiolus symbiont genomes had more mobile elements compared to their closest relatives.
source: The Bathymodiolus symbiont genomes had more mobile elements compared to their closest relatives (Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: This is based on annotation data shown in Supplementary file 1A.

claim: Bathymodiolus symbionts had between 13 and 23 transposases and three to five integrases.
source: Bathymodiolus symbionts had between 13 and 23 transposases and three to five integrases.
evidence: This is based on genome annotation.

claim: SUP05 had 14 transposases and one integrase.
source: SUP05 had 14 transposases and one integrase.
evidence: This is based on genome annotation.

claim: No transposases or integrases were found in the clam symbiont genomes.
source: We did not find any transposases or integrases in the clam symbiont genomes.
evidence: This is based on genome annotation.

claim: The Bathymodiolus symbionts were highly enriched in restriction-modification system genes (between 10 and 22 genes).
source: The Bathymodiolus symbionts were highly enriched in restriction-modification system genes (between 10 and 22 genes), whereas SUP05 only had one, and the clam symbionts had none.
evidence: This is based on genome annotation.

claim: SUP05 only had one restriction-modification system gene.
source: The Bathymodiolus symbionts were highly enriched in restriction-modification system genes (between 10 and 22 genes), whereas SUP05 only had one, and the clam symbionts had none.
evidence: This is based on genome annotation.

claim: The clam symbionts had no restriction-modification system genes.
source: The Bathymodiolus symbionts were highly enriched in restriction-modification system genes (between 10 and 22 genes), whereas SUP05 only had one, and the clam symbionts had none.
evidence: This is based on genome annotation.

claim: Between 2.3 and 7.6% of the genes found only in the Bathymodiolus SOX symbionts but not in the clam symbionts and SUP05 genomes were annotated as toxin or virulence genes.
source: Between 2.3 and 7.6% of the genes found only in the Bathymodiolus SOX symbionts but not in the clam symbionts and SUP05, genomes were annotated as toxin or virulence genes (Figure 2).
evidence: This is based on comparative genomic analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: Most toxin-related genes in Bathymodiolus SOX symbionts were related to genes from three toxin classes: RTX toxins, MARTX toxins, and YD repeat toxins.
source: Most were related to genes from one of three toxin classes: (1) the RTX (repeats in toxins) toxins, (2) MARTX (multifunctional autoprocessing RTX toxins), a sub-group of RTX toxins, and (3) YD repeat toxins (also called rhs genes as they were initially described as 'recombination hotspots').
evidence: This is based on annotation and classification of the TRGs.

claim: Representatives from all three toxin-related gene classes were found in each of the three draft genomes, except for RTX, which were not found in BazSymA.
source: Representatives from all three toxin-related genes (TRGs) classes were found in each of the three-draft genomes, except for RTX, which were not found in BazSymA.
evidence: This is based on genome annotation.

claim: BspSym had at least 33 YD repeat genes, eight RTX genes, and 19 MARTX-like genes.
source: We found the largest number of TRGs in the genome with the fewest contigs, BspSym, which had at least 33 YD repeat genes, eight RTX genes, and 19 MARTX-like genes.
evidence: This is based on genome annotation.

claim: BazSymB had 14 YD repeat genes, two RTX genes, and up to 10 MARTX genes.
source: In the BazSymB genome, 14 YD repeat genes, two RTX genes, and up to 10 MARTX genes were found.
evidence: This is based on genome annotation.

claim: BazSymA had 16 YD repeat genes and one MARTX.
source: BazSymA had 16 YD repeat genes, and one MARTX (Figure 2, Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: This is based on genome annotation shown in Figure 2 and Supplementary file 1B.

claim: In the BspSym genome, 22 out of 88 TRGs were found directly upstream or downstream of mobile elements.
source: In the BspSym genome, which assembled into the largest contigs, 22 out of 88 TRGs were found directly upstream or downstream of mobile elements.
evidence: This is based on genome annotation and analysis.

claim: YD repeat sequences from the symbionts of both Bathymodiolus species formed a distinct cluster, distant from all other sequences in public databases.
source: YD repeat sequences from the symbionts of both Bathymodiolus species formed a distinct cluster, distant from all other sequences in public databases (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The Bathymodiolus symbiont YD repeat sequences did not cluster according to their host species, but instead were intermixed.
source: The Bathymodiolus symbiont sequences did not cluster according to their host species, but instead were intermixed, suggesting gene duplication events prior to the divergence of the B. azoricus and B. sp. symbiont lineages.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: The Bathymodiolus symbiont YD repeat sequences fell into a cluster that contained mostly pathogenic bacteria such as Yersinia pestis and Burkholderia pseudomallei.
source: The Bathymodiolus symbiont sequences fell into a cluster that contained mostly pathogenic bacteria such as Yersinia pestis and Burkholderia pseudomallei.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: The cluster containing Bathymodiolus symbiont YD repeat sequences was well supported by Bayesian analysis (0.91 posterior probability).
source: This cluster was well supported by Bayesian analysis (0.91 posterior probability).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The cluster containing Bathymodiolus symbiont YD repeat sequences also contained beneficial symbionts such as B. rhizoxinica and the Photorhabdus and Xenorhabdus symbionts of soil nematodes.
source: This cluster also contained a number of beneficial symbionts such as B. rhizoxinica, which is an intracellular symbiont of the fungus Rhizopus, and the Photorhabdus and Xenorhabdus symbionts of soil nematodes (Waterfield et al., 2001; Goodrich-Blair and Clarke, 2007; Moebius et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 3 and supported by citations.

claim: The Bathymodiolus symbiont genomes encoded more YD repeat and MARTX genes than any other genome compared.
source: The Bathymodiolus symbiont genomes encoded more YD repeat and MARTX genes than any other genome that we compared them to (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: This is based on comparative analysis shown in Figure 5 and supplements.

claim: MARTX genes were significantly enriched in the genomes of pathogenic vs non-pathogenic bacteria.
source: One class, MARTX was significantly enriched in the genomes of pathogenic vs non-pathogenic bacteria (p-value = 0.007, Kruskal–Wallis test).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis presented in Table 2.

claim: There was a significant bias in the distribution of genes encoding MARTX and YD repeat genes in bacteria according to their lifestyle (extracellular host-associated, intracellular host-associated, or free-living).
source: There was also a significant bias in the distribution of genes encoding MARTX and YD repeat genes in bacteria according to their lifestyle (extracellular host-associated, intracellular host-associated, or free-living).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis presented in Table 2.

claim: Both YD repeat and MARTX genes were enriched in the genomes of host-associated microbes.
source: These showed that both YD repeat and MARTX genes were enriched in the genomes of host-associated microbes (YD repeat: p-value = 0.026, MARTX: p-values = 2.125e−6, 1.618e−6, Mann–Whitney–Wilcoxon test).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis presented in Table 3.

claim: YD repeat genes were only significantly enriched in intracellular bacteria.
source: While MARTX genes were enriched in host-associated bacteria regardless of their location, YD repeat genes were only significantly enriched in intracellular bacteria.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis presented in Table 3.

claim: RTX genes did not show any enrichment in the three defined categories (free-living, extracellular host-associated, intracellular host-associated).
source: In contrast to YD repeat and MARTX genes, RTX did not show any enrichment in the three defined categories.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis.

claim: RTX genes are widely distributed among bacteria and are just as likely to be found in free-living and host-associated bacteria.
source: RTX are therefore widely distributed among bacteria and are just as likely to be found in free-living and host-associated bacteria (Appendix 2).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis and discussed in Appendix 2.

claim: 63–68% of the TRGs could be identified as potentially horizontally acquired based on codon usage analysis.
source: Firstly, 63–68% of the TRGs could be identified as potentially horizontally acquired based on codon usage analysis, in contrast to 30–35% predicted for all coding sequences (Table 1, Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on codon usage analysis.

claim: All predicted TRGs of the SOX symbionts in B. azoricus and B. sp gills were expressed.
source: Transcriptome sequencing revealed that all predicted TRGs of the SOX symbionts in B. azoricus and B. sp gills were expressed.
evidence: This is based on transcriptome analysis.

claim: Reads mapping to TRGs accounted for 0.67–1.71% of mRNA in B. azoricus symbionts.
source: Reads mapping to TRGs accounted for 0.67–1.71% of mRNA in B. azoricus symbionts and 0.58–3.14% in B. sp. symbionts.
evidence: This is based on transcriptome analysis.

claim: Reads mapping to TRGs accounted for 0.58–3.14% of mRNA in B. sp. symbionts.
source: Reads mapping to TRGs accounted for 0.67–1.71% of mRNA in B. azoricus symbionts and 0.58–3.14% in B. sp. symbionts.
evidence: This is based on transcriptome analysis.

claim: The expression levels of some TRGs were in some cases higher than the expression of the essential Calvin cycle gene ribulose bisphosphate carboxylase/oxidase (RuBisCO).
source: The expression levels of some genes from the RTX, MARTX, and YD repeats classes were in some cases higher than the expression of the essential Calvin cycle gene ribulose bisphosphate carboxylase/oxidase (RuBisCO), which accounted for 0.03–0.5% of mRNA in B. azoricus symbionts and 0.11–1.04% in B. sp. symbionts.
evidence: This is based on transcriptome analysis.

claim: In B. azoricus proteomes, 12 YD repeat proteins and one RTX were found.
source: In these proteomes, we found 12 YD repeat proteins and one RTX.
evidence: This is based on proteome analysis shown in Table 4.

claim: In B. azoricus proteomes, one RTX activator and two RTX toxin transporters were found.
source: We also found a number of toxin-associated proteins such as one RTX activator and two RTX toxin transporters (Table 4).
evidence: This is based on proteome analysis shown in Table 4.

claim: Nine of the 12 identified YD repeat proteins were present in the membrane proteome.
source: Nine of the 12 identified YD repeat proteins were present in the membrane proteome.
evidence: This is based on proteome analysis.

claim: One RTX activator and one YD repeat protein were significantly enriched in the host tissue.
source: One RTX activator and one YD repeat protein were significantly enriched in the host tissue (Table 4).
evidence: This is based on proteome analysis shown in Table 4.

claim: The TRGs were most likely acquired by HGT.
source: Considering these observations, and the absence of these TRGs in their close relatives, we consider it most likely that they were acquired through HGT.
evidence: This is based on multiple lines of evidence including codon usage, mobile elements, and phylogenetic analysis.

claim: One of the regions encoding MARTX genes from the Bathymodiolus SOX symbiont has a domain structure similar to the filamentous hemagglutinin FhaB from B. pertussis and Bordetella bronchiseptica.
source: One of the regions encoding MARTX genes from the Bathymodiolus SOX symbiont has a domain structure similar to the filamentous hemagglutinin FhaB from B. pertussis and Bordetella bronchiseptica (MARTX1, see Appendix 3).
evidence: This is based on domain structure analysis discussed in Appendix 3.

claim: FhaB is involved in attachment of Bordetella to their human host and suppression of the immune response.
source: FhaB is involved in attachment of Bordetella to their human host and suppression of the immune response (reviewed by Melvin et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Melvin et al., 2014.

claim: Multiple strains of SOX symbionts can co-occur in Bathymodiolus mussels.
source: Multiple strains of SOX symbionts can co-occur in Bathymodiolus mussels (Won et al., 2003a; DeChaine et al., 2006; Duperron et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Won et al., 2003a; DeChaine et al., 2006; Duperron et al., 2008.

claim: Bathymodiolus mussels are infected by bacterial intranuclear pathogens called Candidatus Endonucleobacter bathymodioli.
source: Bathymodiolus mussels are also infected by bacterial intranuclear pathogens called Candidatus Endonucleobacter bathymodioli, which are related to the genus Endozoicomonas (Zielinski et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zielinski et al., 2009.

claim: Ca. E. bathymodioli invades the mussel cell nuclei where it multiplies, eventually bursting the infected cell.
source: Ca. E. bathymodioli invades the mussel cell nuclei where it multiplies, eventually bursting the infected cell.
evidence: This is based on knowledge from Zielinski et al., 2009.

claim: Intranuclear bacteria are never found in the nuclei of symbiont-containing cells.
source: Intranuclear bacteria are never found in the nuclei of symbiont-containing cells, which led Zielinski et al. (2009) to hypothesize that the symbionts can protect their host cells against infection.
evidence: This is based on observations from Zielinski et al., 2009.

claim: Growth inhibition assays showed that B. azoricus gill tissue homogenates inhibit the growth of a broader spectrum of pathogens compared to the symbiont-free foot tissues.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, growth inhibition assays showed that B. azoricus gill tissue homogenates inhibit the growth of a broader spectrum of pathogens compared to the symbiont-free foot tissues (Bettencourt et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bettencourt et al., 2007.

claim: There is no evidence from the SOX symbiont genomes that they produce antibiotics.
source: There is no evidence from their genomes that the SOX symbionts of B. sp. and B. azoricus produce antibiotics, but they do have genes for bacteriocin production that were expressed in the six transcriptomes analyzed in this study.
evidence: This is based on genome annotation and transcriptome analysis.

claim: The SOX symbionts have genes for bacteriocin production that were expressed in the six transcriptomes analyzed.
source: There is no evidence from their genomes that the SOX symbionts of B. sp. and B. azoricus produce antibiotics, but they do have genes for bacteriocin production that were expressed in the six transcriptomes analyzed in this study.
evidence: This is based on genome annotation and transcriptome analysis.

claim: The genomes of the SOX symbionts of hydrothermal vent Riftia tubeworms and the heterotrophic symbionts of whale-fall Osedax worms only contain one or a few RTX genes, and no YD repeat genes.
source: For example, the genomes of the SOX symbionts of hydrothermal vent Riftia tubeworms and the heterotrophic symbionts of whale-fall Osedax worms are virtually complete, but they only contain one or a few RTX genes, and no YD repeat genes (Robidart et al., 2008; Gardebrecht et al., 2012; Goffredi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Robidart et al., 2008; Gardebrecht et al., 2012; Goffredi et al., 2014.

claim: Candidatus Hamiltonella defensa is a facultative symbiont of aphids that protects its host from attack by parasitic wasps.
source: Both symbionts encode multiple copies of RTX and YD repeat proteins (Degnan and Moran, 2008). Ca. Hamiltonella defensa is a defensive symbiont that protects its host from attack by parasitic wasps (Oliver et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Oliver et al., 2003 and Degnan and Moran, 2008.

claim: The protective effect of Ca. Hamiltonella defensa is linked to its complement of RTX and YD repeat toxins.
source: Its protective effect is linked to its complement of RTX and YD repeat toxins (Degnan and Moran, 2008; Oliver et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Degnan and Moran, 2008 and Oliver et al., 2010.

claim: The most abundant parasites in Bathymodiolus mussels resembled Bucephalus-like trematodes of the phylum Platyhelminthes.
source: The most abundant parasites resembled Bucephalus-like trematodes of the phylum Platyhelminthes, which are common in shallow-water mussels (e.g., Wardle, 1988; Lauenstein et al., 1993; da Silva et al., 2002; Minguez et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on microscopic studies cited from Powell et al., 1999 and Ward et al., 2004.

claim: Bucephalus trematodes infect the gonads of their mussel hosts, which often results in sterilization.
source: Bucephalus trematodes infect the gonads of their mussel hosts, which often results in sterilization (Hopkins, 1957; Coustau et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hopkins, 1957 and Coustau et al., 1991.

claim: Bucephalus-like trematodes were abundant in the gonads of Bathymodiolus childressi from cold seeps in the Gulf of Mexico.
source: Like their shallow-water relatives, the Bucephalus-like trematodes were abundant in the gonads of Bathymodiolus childressi from cold seeps in the Gulf of Mexico (Powell et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Powell et al., 1999.

claim: Up to 40% of B. childressi populations are reproductively compromised due to trematode infection.
source: Powell et al. (1999) estimated that due to this heavy infection, up to 40% of B. childressi populations are reproductively compromised.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Powell et al., 1999.

claim: Of the three Bathymodiolus species studied for parasites, only B. childressi was infected by trematodes.
source: However, of the three species so far studied, only B. childressi was infected by trematodes (Powell et al., 1999; Ward et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Powell et al., 1999 and Ward et al., 2004.

claim: B. childressi is one of the few Bathymodiolus species that only associates with MOX symbionts, but not with SOX symbionts.
source: B. childressi is one of the few Bathymodiolus species that only associates with MOX symbionts, but not with SOX symbionts.
evidence: This is stated as a known fact about B. childressi.

claim: The MOX symbionts of B. azoricus and B. childressi do not encode the abundant TRGs of the Bathymodiolus SOX symbiont.
source: The MOX symbionts of B. azoricus and B. childressi do not encode the abundant TRGs of the Bathymodiolus SOX symbiont (Antony CP, personal communication, May 2015).
evidence: This is based on personal communication cited in the text.

claim: Eight out of nine genes in the MARTX1 region do not have a significantly larger number of SNPs per kb compared to the rest of the genome.
source: Consistent with this, eight out of nine genes in the MARTX1 region, which we hypothesize may be involved in attachment to the host, do not have a significantly larger number of SNPs per kb compared to the rest of the genome (Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on SNP analysis shown in Figure 6 and source data.

claim: 22 TRGs had significantly more SNPs than most of the other genes in the genomes.
source: However, we found 22 TRGs that did have significantly more SNPs than most of the other genes in the genomes.
evidence: This is based on SNP analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: The Bathymodiolus SOX symbiont may play an essential role in both nutrition and defense.
source: The Bathymodiolus symbiont is therefore unusual, as it may play an essential role in both nutrition and defense.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data and discussion.

claim: The Bathymodiolus SOX symbionts encode a larger complement of TRGs than any so far sequenced pathogen.
source: Remarkably, the Bathymodiolus SOX symbionts encode a larger complement of these TRGs than any so far sequenced pathogen, suggesting that these 'toxins', although initially discovered in pathogens, may in fact belong to larger protein families that function in both beneficial and pathogenic host-microbe interactions.
evidence: This is based on comparative analysis shown in Figure 5.
